model_raw_board_events.text: Why Decomposition Matters: Nature's Recycling Plant
Decomposition is nature's recycling plant: it breaks down dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances that producers can reuse.
Detritus = dead organic matter: fallen leaves, bark, flowers, dead animal remains, and faecal matter.
Detritus exists in two layers: above-ground (leaf litter, animal remains) and below-ground (dead roots, remains of underground animals).

model_raw_board_events.text: Humification and Mineralisation
Humification is the accumulation of humus, a dark, amorphous, colloidal substance that is highly resistant to microbial action and acts as a nutrient reservoir.
Mineralisation is the breakdown of humus by microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients back into the soil for plants to use.
Humification stores nutrients; mineralisation releases them. They are opposite in direction.

segment_title: Why Energy Flow is Unidirectional
segment_objective: Explain why energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional and non-cyclic, using the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

model_raw_board_events.text: Why Energy Flow is Unidirectional
Energy flow is the unidirectional movement and transformation of energy through an ecosystem, from the Sun to producers to consumers.
Money circulates in a market, but energy does not. Energy enters once from the Sun, moves in one direction, and leaves as heat at every step.

model_raw_board_events.text: The Sun's Budget: PAR and Producer Capture
Sun is the ultimate energy source for most ecosystems. But not all sunlight is usable by plants.
PAR (Photosynthetically Active Radiation) = the fraction of incident solar radiation usable in photosynthesis. It is less than 50% of total incident radiation.

model_raw_board_events.text: The 10% Law and Trophic Level Calculations
Lindeman's 10% law (1942): only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; ~90% is lost as heat via respiration.
Analogy: commission agents in a market - each keeps 90%, passes 10% up the line.

model_raw_board_events.text: Ecological Pyramids: Number, Biomass, and Energy
Ecological pyramids (Elton, 1927) are graphical representations of number, biomass, or energy at successive trophic levels, with producers at the base.
Pyramid of numbers: count of individuals per unit area at each trophic level.
Pyramid of biomass: standing crop mass (g m^-2) at each trophic level.

Pyramids of number and biomass are usually upright, but can invert in certain ecosystems.
Inverted Pyramid of Numbers: Parasitic Food Chain
Example: A single banyan tree supports thousands of leaf-eating insects, which host even more parasitic mites.

segment_title: Limitations of Ecological Pyramids

model_raw_board_events.text: Limitations of Ecological Pyramids
Pyramids are simplified models, not perfect representations of an ecosystem.
Limitation 1: Pyramids assume a simple linear food chain, but real ecosystems have food webs with many interlinked chains.

model_raw_board_events.text: Grazing Food Chain (GFC) vs Detritus Food Chain (DFC)
GFC starts with living producers. Example: grass → deer → tiger.
DFC starts with dead organic matter (detritus). Example: detritus → earthworm → bird.

segment_title: Exam Traps and Quick Problem Solving
segment_objective: Apply the concepts to solve typical exam questions, including 10% law calculations and pyramid orientation identification.

model_raw_board_events.text: Exam Traps and Quick Problem Solving
Trap 1: Miscounting trophic levels. 'Secondary consumer' is the 3rd trophic level, so apply the 10% law twice. 'Tertiary consumer' is the 4th, so apply it three times.
Trap 2: Confusing PAR with capture efficiency. PAR is less than 50% of incident radiation; producers capture only 2-10% of PAR. These are two different numbers.
Trap 3: Thinking energy cycles. Energy flows one-way and is lost as heat; it never re-enters. Only nutrients cycle.

model_raw_board_events.text: Primary vs Secondary Succession
Primary succession begins on a site where no community ever existed, such as bare rock, cooled lava, or new sand dunes. There is no soil, so it is slow.
Secondary succession begins where a community was present but got wiped out, such as a burned forest or abandoned farmland. Soil and seeds survive, so it is faster.

model_raw_board_events.text: Xerarch Succession: From Bare Rock to Forest
Xerarch succession starts on bare rock with no soil. The pioneer community is crustose lichens.
Crustose lichens secrete organic acids that weather the rock and trap dust, beginning soil formation.
Foliose lichens (e.g., Parmelia) spread over the thin soil, add organic matter, and improve water retention.

Ecosystem: a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact with each other and with their non-living environment, functioning as a unit.

segment_title: Functional Features: The Four Pillars

model_raw_board_events.text: Functional Features: The Four Pillars
Structure = what is there (species composition, stratification). Function = what happens (processes that keep the ecosystem running).
The four functional aspects of an ecosystem are: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, and nutrient cycling.
Productivity is the rate of biomass (organic matter) production per unit area per unit time.

segment_title: Productivity: GPP, NPP, and the Respiration Link
segment_objective: Define GPP and NPP, and apply the relation NPP = GPP - R.

model_raw_board_events.text: Productivity: GPP, NPP, and the Respiration Link
Gross Primary Productivity (GPP): Total rate of energy (or biomass) captured by producers via photosynthesis.
Net Primary Productivity (NPP): Rate of energy (or biomass) remaining after subtracting producer respiration (R). This is what is available to heterotrophs.

Measured as dry weight because water content varies and would distort fresh-weight comparisons.
Standing state: amount of nutrients (e.g., N, P, C) present in the soil at a given time.

model_raw_board_events.text: Trophic Levels and the 10% Law
Trophic level: the position an organism occupies in a food chain based on its source of nutrition. Producers = 1st, herbivores = 2nd, carnivores = 3rd, etc.
Lindeman's 10% law (1942): only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; ~90% is lost as heat via respiration and metabolic activity.

segment_title: Grazing vs Detritus Food Chains
segment_objective: Distinguish between grazing food chain (GFC) and detritus food chain (DFC) with examples and identify which dominates in terrestrial vs aquatic ecosystems.

model_raw_board_events.text: Grazing vs Detritus Food Chains
Grazing Food Chain (GFC): starts with living producers. Example: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake.
Detritus Food Chain (DFC): starts with dead organic matter (detritus). Example: detritus → earthworm → sparrow → falcon.

segment_title: Food Webs: Interconnected Chains
segment_objective: Explain how food chains interconnect to form food webs and why food webs are more realistic.

model_raw_board_events.text: Food Webs: Interconnected Chains
A food web is a network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
Real ecosystems are not simple linear chains; organisms often feed at multiple trophic levels.

segment_title: Ecological Pyramids: Number, Biomass, Energy
segment_objective: Describe the three types of ecological pyramids and state which can be inverted.

model_raw_board_events.text: Ecological Pyramids (Elton, 1927)
Graphical representation of number, biomass, or energy at successive trophic levels, with producers at the base.
Pyramid of number: count of individuals per unit area at each trophic level.
Pyramid of biomass: mass of living material (standing crop) at each trophic level, in g per square metre.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Pyramid of number: producers at base, fewer at each higher level.

segment_title: Pyramid Inversions and Exam Traps
segment_objective: Identify scenarios where pyramids of number and biomass invert and explain why energy pyramid never inverts.

model_raw_board_events.text: Pyramid Inversions and Exam Traps
Pyramids of number and biomass can invert in certain ecosystems, but the pyramid of energy is always upright.
Inverted pyramid of number: single large tree (banyan) supports many insects, which support even more parasites.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Number and biomass can invert; energy never does.

segment_title: The Reservoir: Where Phosphorus Lives
segment_objective: Identify the main reservoir of phosphorus and explain why the cycle is classified as sedimentary.

model_raw_board_events.text: The Reservoir: Where Phosphorus Lives
Every nutrient cycle has a reservoir - a large storehouse from which the nutrient is drawn and to which it returns.
Gaseous cycles: reservoir is atmosphere or hydrosphere. Examples: carbon, nitrogen.
Sedimentary cycles: reservoir is Earth's crust or rocks. Examples: phosphorus, sulphur.

model_raw_board_events.text: Weathering: Releasing Phosphorus from Rock
Phosphorus is locked in rock as phosphate minerals (the reservoir).
Weathering is the slow breakdown of rock that releases phosphate ions into the soil solution.

model_raw_board_events.text: Uptake and the Food Chain
Plants absorb phosphate ions (PO4^3-) from the soil solution through their roots.
Phosphorus is a limiting nutrient in many ecosystems, meaning its scarcity limits plant growth.
Once inside the plant, phosphorus is used to make ATP, DNA, RNA, and phospholipids in cell membranes.

segment_title: Exam Traps and Quick Revision
segment_objective: Identify common exam pitfalls and recall key points about the phosphorus cycle.

model_raw_board_events.text: Phosphorus Cycle: Exam Traps & Quick Revision
Biggest trap: phosphorus has NO gaseous phase and NO respiratory release. Do not confuse with carbon cycle.
Reservoir of phosphorus is rock (Earth's crust), not atmosphere. This makes it a sedimentary cycle.
Mnemonic: 'PuSS is Sedimentary' — Phosphorus and Sulphur are sedimentary; Carbon and Nitrogen are gaseous.

segment_title: What is Productivity?
segment_objective: Define productivity as a rate of biomass production per unit area per unit time and distinguish it from standing crop.

model_raw_board_events.text: Productivity vs Standing Crop
Productivity is the rate of biomass (organic matter) production per unit area per unit time.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Productivity is a rate; standing crop is a stock.

segment_title: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)
segment_objective: Define GPP as the total rate of photosynthesis by producers and identify its units.

model_raw_board_events.text: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)
GPP is the total rate of organic matter (biomass) production by producers through photosynthesis, including the portion later used in respiration.
Think of GPP as the gross income of the producer: all energy captured before any running costs are paid.

segment_title: Net Primary Productivity (NPP)
segment_objective: Calculate NPP using NPP = GPP − R and explain its significance as energy available to heterotrophs.

model_raw_board_events.text: Net Primary Productivity (NPP)
NPP is the organic matter left with producers after their own respiratory loss. It is the biomass actually available to heterotrophs.
R is the respiratory loss by the producers only, not by decomposers.

segment_title: Secondary Productivity
segment_objective: Define secondary productivity as the rate of new organic matter formation by consumers and explain why it is smaller than primary productivity.

model_raw_board_events.text: Secondary Productivity
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers (heterotrophs).
Consumers receive NPP as their energy income, spend their own respiration, and pass on only a fraction to the next level.

segment_title: Units and Measurement of Productivity
segment_objective: State the units of productivity and explain why dry mass is used for measurement.

model_raw_board_events.text: Units and Measurement of Productivity
Productivity is a rate: biomass produced per unit area per unit time.
Units: mass form: g m⁻² yr⁻¹; energy form: kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Productivity is a rate; standing crop is a stock.

segment_title: Factors Affecting Primary Productivity
segment_objective: List the main factors limiting primary productivity in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

model_raw_board_events.text: Factors Affecting Primary Productivity
Primary productivity is limited by internal plant factors and external environmental factors.
Internal factors: availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity of the plants.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Internal vs external factors

segment_title: Common Traps and Exam Application
segment_objective: Apply the productivity concepts to solve typical NEET/CUET/Board questions, avoiding common pitfalls.

model_raw_board_events.text: Common Traps and Exam Application
Trap 1: Productivity vs Standing Crop. Productivity is a rate (per area per time). Standing crop is the biomass present at a given time. Watch for 'rate of' vs 'amount at a time'.
Trap 2: The Respiration Trap. NPP = GPP - R, where R is the producers' own respiration. Not GPP minus decomposition, and definitely not GPP + R. Decomposers do not enter this equation.

Trap 3: Structure vs Function. Species composition and stratification are structural. Productivity, decomposition, energy flow, and nutrient cycling are functional. Examiners love planting 'stratification is a functional unit' as a false statement.

model_raw_board_events.caption: Productivity is a rate; standing crop is a stock.
